    24	\DeclareMathOperator{\Div}{Div}
    25	\DeclareMathOperator{\Princ}{Princ}

    27	% Standard operators used: \deg, \dim, \sup. Standard amssymb symbols: \mathbb, \mathbf.
    28	
    29	\begin{document}
    30	
    31	\noindent
    32	We may let $v_P : \Div(\mathbb{F}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ be defined by
    33	$v_P(D) = n_P$, the $P$'th coefficient of $D$. A partial ordering $\leq$ on
    34	$\Div(\mathbb{F})$ can be introduced by writing $D_1 \leq D_2$ if and only if
    35	$v_P(D_1) \leq v_P(D_2)$ for all $P \in \mathbf{P}$. A divisor $D$ is called
    36	\emph{effective} if it is non-negative, in the sense that $D \geq 0$. Since the
    37	formal sums are finite, we have a notion of \emph{degree} for divisors: if
    38	\[
    39	  D = \sum_{P \in \mathbf{P}_{\mathbb{F}}} n_P P,
    40	\]
    41	then we may define
    42	\[
    43	  \deg(D) = \sum_{p \in \mathbf{P}_{\mathbb{F}}} v_P(D) \deg(P).
    44	\]
    45	The degree map is actually a homomorphism $\Div(\mathbb{F}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$.
    46	
    47	\begin{definition}[1.7]
    48	Let $x \in \mathbb{F}^*$ and denote by $Z$ the set of zeroes of $x$ in
    49	$\mathbf{P}_{\mathbb{F}}$. Then, we define the zero divisor of $x$ to be
    50	\[
    51	  (x)_0 = \sum_{P \in Z} v_P(x) P \in \Div(\mathbb{F});
    52	\]
    53	analogously, if $N$is the set of poles of $x$, we define the pole divisor of $x$
    54	as $(x)_\infty = \sum_{P \in N}(-v_P(x))P$. Finally, the principal divisor of $x$
    55	is defined to be
    56	\[
    57	  (x) = (x)_0 - (x)_\infty = \sum_{P \in \mathbf{P}_{\mathbb{F}}} v_P(x) P.
    58	\]
    59	\end{definition}
    60	
    61	IN what follows, we will he assumption that $K$ is algebraically closed will now
    62	imply that a non-zero element $x \in \mathbb{F}$ is constant if and only if
    63	$(x) = 0$; this follows from the fact that any $z \in \mathbb{F}$ which is
    64	transcendental over $\mathbb{K}$ has at least one zero and one pole and
    65	Theorem 1.1.
    66	
    67	\begin{definition}[1.8]
    68	The subgroup $\Princ(\mathbb{F}) = \{(x) \mid x \in \mathbb{F}^*\}$ of
    69	$\Div(\mathbb{F})$ is called the group of principal divisors of
    70	$\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{K}$; the operation in this group is given by
    71	$(xy) = (x) + (y)$. The class group
    72	\[
    73	  \Class(\mathbb{F}) = \Div(\mathbb{F})/\Princ(\mathbb{F})
    74	\]
    75	is called the divisor class group; its elements are classes of the form $[D]$,
    76	where $D \in \Div(\mathbb{F})$ is a representative. Equality of divisor classes
    77	$[D] = [D']$ in $\Class(\mathbb{F})$ induces an equivalence relation $D \sim D'$ in
    78	$\Div(\mathbb{F})$. Therefore, $D \sim D'$ if and only if the difference $D - D'$
    79	is some principal divisor $(x)$.
    80	\end{definition}
    81	
    82	Another object we need to introduce is the following class of $K$-vector spaces.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[1.9]
    85	For a divisor $D \in \Div(\mathbb{F})$, we let
    86	\[
    87	  L(A) = \{x \in \mathbb{F}^* \mid (x) \geq -D\} \cup \{0\}.
    88	\]
    89	\end{definition}
    90	
    91	\noindent
    92	\emph{Explicitly, if $v_P(D) > 0$ when and only when $P \in I$, where $I$ is a
    93	finite subset of $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbb{F}}$ and $v_Q(D) < 0$ when and only when
    94	$Q \in J$, where $J$ is a finite subset of $\Div(\mathbb{F})$, then $L(D)$ contains
    95	all $x \in \mathbb{F}^*$ such that $x$ has zeroes of order at least $-v_Q(D)$ at
    96	all elements $Q \in J$ and poles of order at most $v_Q(D)$ at all elements
    97	$P \in I$.}
    98	
    99	It's now obvious that $L(D)$ is a $K$-vector space, and all equivalent divisors
   100	have isomorphic corresponding vector spaces (for this second assertion, assume
   101	that $D \sim D'$ and then let $\phi : L(D) \longrightarrow L(D')$ be given by
   102	$x \mapsto xz$, where $z$ is the fixed element of $\mathbb{F}$ such that
   103	$D = D' + (z)$).
   104	
   105	Our next objective will be to show that $\dim_{\mathbb{K}} L(D)$ is finite for all
   106	divisors $D$ of $\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{K}$. This is intimately connected with the fact
   107	that the \textbf{genus} of $\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{K}$, is in fact well-defined and
   108	finite.
   109	
   110	\begin{definition}[1.10]
   111	The genus $g$ of a function field $\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{K}$ is defined by
   112	\[
   113	  g = \sup\{\deg D - \dim D + 1 \mid D \in \Div(\mathbb{F})\}.
   114	\]
   115	\end{definition}
   116	
   117	\noindent
   118	\emph{Note that this definition is legitimate (the supremum in question exists)
   119	since the difference $\deg D - \dim D$ is bounded above, by the previous theorem.}

  supplied by the cited proposition alone.

\provenancetag{ADAPTED}
  The \emph{genus} of a smooth proper curve \(C\) over \(k\) is
  \[
    g(C) \;=\; \dim_k H^1\!\bigl(C, \struct C\bigr),
  \]
  the \(k\)-dimension of the first cohomology group of the structure sheaf, viewed as a sheaf
  of \(k\)-modules on the small Zariski site of \(C\) (Definition~\ref{def:moduleKSheaf}),
  with cohomology the \(\Ext\)-groups from the constant sheaf
  (Definition~\ref{def:HModule}).
